claim: Nearly all mitochondrial proteins need to be targeted for import from the cytosol.
source: Nearly all mitochondrial proteins need to be targeted for import from the cytosol.
evidence: This is a general statement about mitochondrial protein import that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: For the majority of mitochondrial proteins, the first port of call is the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM complex).
source: For the majority, the first port of call is the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM complex), followed by a procession of alternative molecular machines, conducting transport to their final destination.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial protein import pathways.

claim: The pre-sequence translocase of the inner membrane (TIM23-complex) imports proteins with cleavable pre-sequences.
source: The pre-sequence translocase of the inner membrane (TIM23-complex) imports proteins with cleavable pre-sequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the TIM23 complex.

claim: Two major rate-limiting steps define PCP import time: passage of PCP across the outer membrane and initiation of inner membrane transport by the pre-sequence.
source: Notably, we found that two major rate-limiting steps define PCP import time: passage of PCP across the outer membrane and initiation of inner membrane transport by the pre-sequence – the rates of which are influenced by PCP size and net charge.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the NanoLuc import assays and kinetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rates of the two major rate-limiting steps are influenced by PCP size and net charge.
source: Notably, we found that two major rate-limiting steps define PCP import time: passage of PCP across the outer membrane and initiation of inner membrane transport by the pre-sequence – the rates of which are influenced by PCP size and net charge.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of varying PCP length and charge on import kinetics.

claim: Passage through TOM is substantially complete before PCP-TIM engagement.
source: The apparent distinction between transport through the two membranes (passage through TOM is substantially complete before PCP-TIM engagement) is in contrast with the current view that import occurs through TOM and TIM in a single continuous step.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing two distinct rate-limiting steps and the effects of varying PCP properties.

claim: PCPs spend very little time in the TIM23 channel.
source: Our results also indicate that PCPs spend very little time in the TIM23 channel – presumably rapid success or failure of import is critical for maintenance of mitochondrial fitness.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing that passage through TIM23 is not rate-limiting.

claim: Rapid success or failure of import is critical for maintenance of mitochondrial fitness.
source: Our results also indicate that PCPs spend very little time in the TIM23 channel – presumably rapid success or failure of import is critical for maintenance of mitochondrial fitness.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed rapid transport through TIM23.

claim: Mitochondria are double membrane-bound eukaryotic organelles responsible for the biosynthesis of ATP among many other essential cellular functions.
source: Mitochondria are double membrane-bound eukaryotic organelles responsible for the biosynthesis of ATP among many other essential cellular functions (Nowinski et al., 2018; Rouault, 2012; Nicholls, 1978; Chen et al., 2003; Nishikawa et al., 2000; Hoth et al., 1997; Chandel, 2015; Wang and Youle, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Of more than a thousand proteins that constitute the mitochondrial proteome, all but a handful (encoded on the mitochondrial genome ‒ 13 in human) are synthesised in the cytosol and must be imported.
source: Of more than a thousand proteins that constitute the mitochondrial proteome, all but a handful (encoded on the mitochondrial genome ‒ 13 in human) are synthesised in the cytosol and must be imported.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial protein composition and import requirements.

claim: Almost all mitochondrial proteins initially enter mitochondria via the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM complex) which contains the pore-forming β-barrel protein Tom40.
source: Almost all mitochondrial proteins (exceptions include precursors of α-helical outer mitochondrial membrane [OMM] proteins) initially enter mitochondria via the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM complex) which contains the pore-forming β-barrel protein Tom40 (Ahting et al., 2001; Guan et al., 2021; Araiso et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Precursors of α-helical outer mitochondrial membrane proteins are exceptions that do not initially enter mitochondria via the TOM complex.
source: Almost all mitochondrial proteins (exceptions include precursors of α-helical outer mitochondrial membrane [OMM] proteins) initially enter mitochondria via the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM complex) which contains the pore-forming β-barrel protein Tom40 (Ahting et al., 2001; Guan et al., 2021; Araiso et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Roughly 60–70% of mitochondrial precursor proteins have a positively charged, amphipathic α-helical pre-sequence.
source: Roughly, 60–70% of mitochondrial precursor proteins – almost all those targeted to the matrix and a subset of IMM proteins – have a positively charged, amphipathic α-helical pre-sequence, also known as a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS; Araiso et al., 2019; Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pre-sequence-containing precursors pass through the TIM23 complex in an unfolded state.
source: Following emergence from the Tom40 channel, these pre-sequence-containing precursors (PCPs) are transferred to the translocase of the inner membrane (TIM23-complex), through which they pass in an unfolded state (Eilers and Schatz, 1986; Matouschek et al., 1997; Neupert and Brunner, 2002; Rassow et al., 1990; Neupert and Herrmann, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The core TIM23CORE comprises three membrane-spanning proteins: Tim23, Tim17, and Tim50.
source: The core (TIM23CORE) comprises three membrane-spanning proteins: Tim23, Tim17, and Tim50 and associates with different proteins to form complexes tailored for different tasks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the TIM23 complex core.

claim: TIM23CORE associates with Tim21 and Mgr2 to form the TIM23SORT complex, capable of lateral release of proteins with hydrophobic sorting sequences.
source: Together with Tim21 and Mgr2, it forms the TIM23SORT complex, capable of lateral release of proteins with hydrophobic sorting sequences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TIM23 complex variants and their functions.

claim: Association of TIM23CORE with the pre-sequence translocase-associated motor (PAM) forms the TIM23MOTOR complex, responsible for matrix import.
source: Association with the pre-sequence translocase-associated motor (PAM) forms the TIM23MOTOR complex, responsible for matrix import.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TIM23 complex variants and their functions.

claim: The electrical component of the proton-motive force across the IMM (membrane potential, ∆ψ; negative in the matrix) is required after entry of the PCP through TOM.
source: After entry of the PCP through TOM, the electrical component of the proton-motive force (PMF) across the IMM – the membrane potential (∆ψ; negative in the matrix) – is required, acting as an electrophoretic force on the positively charged pre-sequence (Martin et al., 1991; Geissler et al., 2000; Truscott et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ∆ψ acts as an electrophoretic force on the positively charged pre-sequence.
source: After entry of the PCP through TOM, the electrical component of the proton-motive force (PMF) across the IMM – the membrane potential (∆ψ; negative in the matrix) – is required, acting as an electrophoretic force on the positively charged pre-sequence (Martin et al., 1991; Geissler et al., 2000; Truscott et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ∆ψ alone is sufficient for insertion of membrane proteins via the TIM23SORT complex.
source: ∆ψ alone is sufficient for insertion of membrane proteins via the TIM23SORT complex (Callegari et al., 2020), but complete import into the matrix by the TIM23MOTOR complex requires an additional driving force: ATP hydrolysis by the main component of PAM, the mtHsp70 protein (Ssc1 in yeast) (Wachter et al., 1994), which pulls the rest of the PCP through to the matrix after the MTS has been imported.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Complete import into the matrix by the TIM23MOTOR complex requires ATP hydrolysis by mtHsp70 protein (Ssc1 in yeast).
source: ∆ψ alone is sufficient for insertion of membrane proteins via the TIM23SORT complex (Callegari et al., 2020), but complete import into the matrix by the TIM23MOTOR complex requires an additional driving force: ATP hydrolysis by the main component of PAM, the mtHsp70 protein (Ssc1 in yeast) (Wachter et al., 1994), which pulls the rest of the PCP through to the matrix after the MTS has been imported.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: mtHsp70 pulls the rest of the PCP through to the matrix after the MTS has been imported.
source: ∆ψ alone is sufficient for insertion of membrane proteins via the TIM23SORT complex (Callegari et al., 2020), but complete import into the matrix by the TIM23MOTOR complex requires an additional driving force: ATP hydrolysis by the main component of PAM, the mtHsp70 protein (Ssc1 in yeast) (Wachter et al., 1994), which pulls the rest of the PCP through to the matrix after the MTS has been imported.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Following passage through or into the IMM, the MTS is cleaved by a matrix processing peptidase.
source: Finally, following passage through or into the IMM, the MTS is cleaved by a matrix processing peptidase (Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The NanoLuc import assay is ∆ψ-dependent.
source: As expected, it is ∆ψ-dependent, affected by depletion of ATP, and sensitive to specific inhibitors of TIM23-dependent protein import (Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by data from the cited previous study.

claim: The NanoLuc import assay is affected by depletion of ATP.
source: As expected, it is ∆ψ-dependent, affected by depletion of ATP, and sensitive to specific inhibitors of TIM23-dependent protein import (Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by data from the cited previous study.

claim: The NanoLuc import assay is sensitive to specific inhibitors of TIM23-dependent protein import.
source: As expected, it is ∆ψ-dependent, affected by depletion of ATP, and sensitive to specific inhibitors of TIM23-dependent protein import (Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by data from the cited previous study.

claim: The concentration of 11S in the mitochondrial matrix ranges from approximately 2.8 to 7.5 µM.
source: The results revealed high (µM) internal 11S concentrations with some variation between mitochondrial preparations (~2.8–7.5 µM; see source data).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative Western blotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Signal amplitude is not limited by 11S concentration.
source: This confirms that signal amplitude is not limited by 11S (see also below) and is a faithful measure of imported PCP, irrespective of how much is added to the outside.
evidence: This is supported by data showing no correlation between 11S concentration and signal amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: 11S is correctly localised in the matrix and not the IMS.
source: Thus, we can conclude that 11S is correctly localised in the matrix and not the IMS.
evidence: This is supported by digitonin extraction experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Signal amplitude is linearly related to PCP concentration from 753 fM up to ~45 nM, where it plateaus.
source: Plotting the results shows that amplitude is linearly related to PCP concentration from 753 fM up to ~45 nM, where it plateaus (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Only a tiny fraction of the PCP added reaches the matrix.
source: Evidently then, only a tiny fraction of the PCP added reaches the matrix.
evidence: This is inferred from the calculation that if all 45 nM PCP were imported, it would correspond to roughly 540 µM inside the matrix, which exceeds the internal 11S concentration.

claim: When DHFR is positioned C-terminal to pep86 with sufficient length between the two to span the TOM and TIM complexes, import signal is observed in the presence of MTX.
source: However, when DHFR is positioned C-terminal to pep86 (PCP-pep86-DHFR) with sufficient length between the two to span the TOM and TIM complexes (212 amino acids in this case, longer than the 135 required [Rassow et al., 1989]), we do see an import signal (Figure 2A, orange bars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NanoLuc can form as soon as pep86 enters the matrix and does not require the entire PCP to be imported.
source: This confirms that NanoLuc can form as soon as pep86 enters the matrix and does not require the entire PCP to be imported, as seen previously with the bacterial Sec system (Allen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data with PCP-pep86-DHFR and comparison to previous work.

claim: The presence or absence of MTX makes only a minor difference to the amplitude of the signal for PCP-pep86-DHFR.
source: Importantly, the presence or absence of MTX makes only a minor difference to the amplitude of this signal (Figure 2A, orange bars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only about 20% of the signal arises from turnovers beyond the first one.
source: The slope, which corresponds to the increase in amplitude per 1 nM PCP-pep86-DHFR, is 1.22 times greater in the absence of MTX, meaning only about 20% of the signal arises from turnovers beyond the first one.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Import behaves as single turnover under the restrictive conditions using isolated mitochondria.
source: Of course, while this does not mean that import is strictly single turnover – which would certainly seem implausible for fully functional mitochondria in their native environment – it does suggest that it behaves as single turnover under the restrictive conditions here, using isolated mitochondria (without the cytosol).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing minimal difference in amplitude with and without MTX.

claim: The amount of PCP-pep86-DHFR that was fully internalised in the matrix in the absence of MTX (11 pmol per mg mitochondria) matched closely the approximate amount of TIM23 dimer estimated to be in the sample of mitochondria (8.5 pmol per mg mitochondrial protein).
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the amount of PCP-pep86-DHFR that was fully internalised in the matrix in the absence of MTX (11 pmol per mg mitochondria, based on quantification of Western blot bands in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) matched closely the approximate amount of TIM23 dimer estimated to be in the sample of mitochondria (8.5 pmol per mg mitochondrial protein [Sirrenberg et al., 1997]).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data and comparison to published values.

claim: Signal amplitude can be reduced by depleting ∆ψ.
source: It has previously been shown that signal amplitude can be reduced by depleting ∆ψ (Pereira et al., 2019), which would suggest that available energy limits protein import.
evidence: This is supported by data from a previous study.

claim: Available energy limits protein import.
source: It has previously been shown that signal amplitude can be reduced by depleting ∆ψ (Pereira et al., 2019), which would suggest that available energy limits protein import.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that depleting ∆ψ reduces signal amplitude.

claim: 'Resetting' the channel after import possibly requires dimerisation of TIM23.
source: This can be reconciled with the apparent single turnover nature of the reaction if 'resetting' the channel after import – possibly through dimerisation of TIM23, as previously reported (Bauer et al., 1996) – requires additional energy input.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on previous reports of TIM23 dimerisation.

claim: Formation of NanoLuc is faster than about 5 min⁻¹ and will not be resolved in the experimental setup.
source: It is also important to note that any additional step faster than about 5 min–1 will not be resolved in our experimental set up – due to the limitations of the plate reader (see detailed explanation in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Instead, the extra step will manifest itself as a small apparent additional lag before the signal appears (equal to 1/kstep, where kstep is the rate constant for that process; Allen et al., 2020). This includes formation of NanoLuc: it is >7.4 min–1 even at the lowest estimated 11S concentration, as determined in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and technical limitations of the measurement system.

claim: Import kinetics are not appreciably affected by the concentration of matrix 11S.
source: Consistent with this, we observe that the import kinetics are not appreciably affected by the concentration of matrix 11S, despite its variance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: k1′ corresponds to transport of the PCP through TOM.
source: However, as detailed below, they can be distinguished by perturbing the system and seeing how this affects the different rates. From this, and based on the results in the following sections, we assign k1′ as transport of the PCP through TOM and k2′ as subsequent engagement of the MTS with the TIM23 complex.
evidence: This assignment is based on experimental data from perturbation experiments and analysis of length and position variants.

claim: k2′ corresponds to subsequent engagement of the MTS with the TIM23 complex.
source: However, as detailed below, they can be distinguished by perturbing the system and seeing how this affects the different rates. From this, and based on the results in the following sections, we assign k1′ as transport of the PCP through TOM and k2′ as subsequent engagement of the MTS with the TIM23 complex.
evidence: This assignment is based on experimental data from perturbation experiments and analysis of length and position variants.

claim: There is no significant difference between any of the four position variants with respect to amplitude, k1′, or k2′.
source: We observe no significant difference between any of the four position variants with respect to any of the three parameters, indicating that transport through TIM23 is fast, and not rate-limiting; therefore, it does not contribute appreciably to the kinetics of import.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Transport through TIM23 is fast and not rate-limiting.
source: We observe no significant difference between any of the four position variants with respect to any of the three parameters, indicating that transport through TIM23 is fast, and not rate-limiting; therefore, it does not contribute appreciably to the kinetics of import.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference between position variants.

claim: Signal amplitude is inversely correlated with protein length for the length variant series.
source: For the length series, signal amplitude is inversely correlated with protein length (Figure 3C, left panel in orange).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Shorter proteins are able to accumulate at higher levels in the matrix compared to large ones.
source: The only plausible explanation is that shorter proteins are able to accumulate at higher levels in the matrix compared to large ones.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amplitude varies with protein length but not with pep86 position.

claim: k1′ has a strong inverse correlation with PCP length.
source: Strikingly, we find that k1ʹ has a strong inverse correlation with PCP length (but not pep86 position), i.e., it is faster for smaller proteins (Figure 3C, middle graph).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The step time (1/k1′) increases exponentially as a function of PCP length.
source: Even more surprisingly, the corresponding step time (1/k1ʹ) increases not linearly but exponentially as a function of PCP length (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Exponential length-dependence is characteristic of an unbiased reversible diffusion-based (passive) mechanism.
source: Exponential length-dependence is not a characteristic of a powered or biased directional transport, such as we have seen previously for the Sec system (Allen et al., 2020), but rather an unbiased reversible diffusion-based (passive) mechanism (Simon et al., 1992).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about transport mechanisms and comparison to previous work.

claim: All three parameters (amplitude, k1′, and k2′) show a dependence on PCP concentration for the length series.
source: Unexpectedly, all three parameters show a dependence on [PCP] for the length series.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The apparent KMs for k1′ are in the low 100s of nM and not systematically dependent on PCP length.
source: The apparent KMs for k1ʹ, (Figure 3E, teal) are in the low 100 s of nM and not systematically dependent on PCP length – this is reasonable for initial association of PCP with TOM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Kds for amplitude and KMs for k2′ are very similar to one another and increase with increasing PCP length.
source: The Kds for amplitude and KMs for k2ʹ, meanwhile (magenta and brown, respectively in Figure 3E), are very similar to one another: they are very low (high affinity) but increase (decrease in affinity) with increasing PCP length.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Amplitude and k2′ reflect the same process, i.e., the final kinetic step of transport.
source: Because amplitude and k2′ behave identically, it seems reasonable to assume that they reflect the same process, i.e., the final kinetic step of transport (because amplitude is, by definition, successful transport).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar concentration dependence of amplitude and k2′.

claim: There is no systematic difference between the position variants in terms of concentration dependence.
source: Just as before, we find no systematic difference between the position variants (Figure 3F) – again suggesting that passage of the PCP through TIM23 is not limiting the overall import rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 10 nM of valinomycin is sufficient to substantially reduce ∆ψ without completely abolishing precursor transport.
source: Mitochondria were pre-treated with valinomycin, a potassium ionophore, which depletes membrane potential in the presence of K+ ions: 10 nM of valinomycin was used – sufficient to substantially reduce ∆ψ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) without completely abolishing precursor transport (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The effect of valinomycin on signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants.
source: The effect on the signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants (Figure 4A, left panel) – in contrast to both apparent rate constants: k1ʹ is somewhat slowed for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones (Figure 4A, middle panel), while k2ʹ is somewhat slowed for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: k1′ is somewhat slowed by valinomycin for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones.
source: The effect on the signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants (Figure 4A, left panel) – in contrast to both apparent rate constants: k1ʹ is somewhat slowed for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones (Figure 4A, middle panel), while k2ʹ is somewhat slowed for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: k2′ is somewhat slowed by valinomycin for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones.
source: The effect on the signal amplitude is roughly the same for all length and position variants (Figure 4A, left panel) – in contrast to both apparent rate constants: k1ʹ is somewhat slowed for shorter proteins but largely unaffected for longer ones (Figure 4A, middle panel), while k2ʹ is somewhat slowed for short proteins but dramatically reduced for longer ones (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Endogenous matrix ATP under conditions of ATP depletion is minimal.
source: Endogenous matrix ATP under these conditions is minimal, as is evident from the fact that import becomes highly sensitive to antimycin A, an inhibitor of oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing sensitivity to antimycin A.

claim: ATP depletion shows reduced amplitude, with this effect being more pronounced for longer PCPs.
source: Import experiments performed with depleted ATP show reduced amplitude, but unlike the response to valinomycin, this effect is more pronounced for the longer PCPs (Figure 4B, left panel) – consistent with the proposed role for ATP in promoting transport of the mature part of the PCP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ATP depletion has little or no effect on k1′.
source: ATP depletion has little or no effect on k1ʹ (Figure 4B, middle panel) and a relatively minor effect on k2ʹ (Figure 4B, right panel), affecting both the length and position variants roughly equally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ATP depletion has a relatively minor effect on k2′.
source: ATP depletion has little or no effect on k1ʹ (Figure 4B, middle panel) and a relatively minor effect on k2ʹ (Figure 4B, right panel), affecting both the length and position variants roughly equally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The concentration dependence of k1′ saturates with an apparent KM of around 100–200 nM.
source: Based on its dependence on PCP concentration (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we assign k1ʹ to the initial interaction between PCP and TOM. However, the concentration dependence of this step saturates with an apparent KM of around 100–200 nM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, the entire PCP passes through TOM before transport through TIM23 is initiated.
source: The strong dependence of k1ʹ on PCP length (Figure 3C, middle panel) provides a clue as to the nature of k1 – it is likely to correspond to passage of the PCP across the OMM, through the TOM complex. The non-linear dependence of step time (1/k1ʹ) on PCP length (Figure 3D) also suggests that this step is at least partially diffusional rather than driven by an active energy-dependent directional motor. Furthermore, it suggests that, under these experimental conditions at least, the entire PCP passes through TOM before transport through TIM23 is initiated.
evidence: This is inferred from the exponential length-dependence of k1′.

claim: k2′ is primarily the ∆ψ-dependent insertion of the pre-sequence through TIM23, not the subsequent passage of the unfolded passenger domain.
source: Since k2ʹ shows very little dependence on PCP length in energised mitochondria (Figure 3C, right panel), we propose that it is primarily the ∆ψ-dependent insertion of the pre-sequence through TIM23, not the subsequent passage of the unfolded passenger domain that is limiting (although both presumably contribute to the apparent rate constant).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of length-dependence of k2′ in energised mitochondria.

claim: Under conditions of ∆ψ depletion, a length-dependence of k2′ emerges.
source: However, under conditions of ∆ψ depletion, a length-dependence of k2ʹ emerges (Figure 4A, right panel, orange open circles).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ∆ψ drives the transport of the mature domain of the precursor, and not exclusively the MTS.
source: This suggests that ∆ψ drives the transport of the mature domain of the precursor, and not exclusively the MTS, and is consistent with the import rate of the rest of the PCP being affected by (∆ψ [Schendzielorz et al., 2017], and see also below).
evidence: This is inferred from the emergence of length-dependence of k2′ under ∆ψ depletion and supported by a citation.

claim: Removal of the OMM should eliminate steps at the OMM (k1) but not at the IMM (k2).
source: To confirm our assignments of k1ʹ and k2ʹ, we tested the effect of removing the OMM (producing mitoplasts) on import kinetics. If the model is correct, this should eliminate steps at the OMM (i.e. k1) but not at the IMM (k2).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: Mitoplasts were isolated from yeast mitochondria using an optimised concentration of 2 mg/ml digitonin.
source: Mitoplasts were isolated from yeast mitochondria using an optimised concentration of 2 mg/ml digitonin, and successful removal of the OMM was confirmed by respirometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: Even without the OMM, a two-step model is required to describe the data.
source: Even without the OMM, a two-step model is required to describe the data; however, while the values for k2ʹ are similar in mitoplasts to those observed in mitochondria (Figure 5), k1ʹ is substantially increased by removal of the OMM for both the shortest (Figure 5A) and longest (Figure 5B) of the length variant PCPs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: k2′ is unaffected by removal of the OMM, confirming that it takes place at the IMM.
source: The fact that k2' is unaffected by removal of the OMM confirms that it takes place at the IMM, as predicted.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing mitochondria and mitoplasts.

claim: k1′ is substantially increased by removal of the OMM.
source: Even without the OMM, a two-step model is required to describe the data; however, while the values for k2ʹ are similar in mitoplasts to those observed in mitochondria (Figure 5), k1ʹ is substantially increased by removal of the OMM for both the shortest (Figure 5A) and longest (Figure 5B) of the length variant PCPs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Signal amplitude is almost completely unaffected by OMM removal for the shortest protein (L).
source: For the shortest protein, L, signal amplitude is almost completely unaffected by OMM removal, while for the longest, DDDL, amplitude is only moderately reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduction in amplitude for the longest protein (DDDL) in mitoplasts is most likely due to a slightly depleted ∆ψ.
source: For the shortest protein, L, signal amplitude is almost completely unaffected by OMM removal, while for the longest, DDDL, amplitude is only moderately reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). Most likely, the latter reduction is due to a slightly depleted ∆ψ in mitoplasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amplitude is reduced for longer proteins in mitoplasts.

claim: Amplitude is strongly inversely correlated with net charge of the PCP.
source: The most immediately striking observation is that amplitude is strongly inversely correlated with net charge of the PCP – the opposite of what might be expected given the direction of ∆ψ (inside negative; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PCPs cause strong depolarisation of ∆ψ, and this effect diminishes with increasing net negative charge.
source: The PCPs did indeed cause strong depolarisation of ∆ψ, and moreover, this effect diminished with increasing net negative charge.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pre-treatment of mitochondria with valinomycin abolishes the correlation between net charge and amplitude.
source: A second prediction from the above hypothesis is that membrane depolarisation prior to protein import will abolish the correlation between net charge and amplitude. This is indeed exactly what we observe: pre-treatment of mitochondria with valinomycin reduces amplitudes for all PCPs, but the effect is greater for more negatively charged PCPs, bringing all amplitudes to about the same level (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Depleting ATP has very little effect on amplitude for the charge variant PCPs.
source: Depleting ATP, meanwhile, has very little effect on amplitude, just as for the Acp1-based PCPs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Positively charged PCPs are imported much faster than negatively charged ones.
source: It is clear from looking directly at the import traces that positively charged PCPs are imported much faster than negatively charged ones (albeit reaching a lower final amplitude; Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The more positively charged PCPs do not show the characteristic delay before signal appears that indicates a two-step transport model.
source: Furthermore, the more positively charged PCPs do not show the characteristic delay before signal appears that indicates a two-step transport model (see Figure 1C); in this case a simpler single-step model is sufficient.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the import traces for positively charged PCPs.

claim: Higher amplitudes are observed for shorter and more negatively charged native PCPs.
source: Consistent with our earlier results, we see higher amplitudes for the shorter and more negatively charged PCPs (Figure 7B), and faster import of the shorter PCPs than the longer ones (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Faster import is observed for shorter native PCPs than longer ones.
source: Consistent with our earlier results, we see higher amplitudes for the shorter and more negatively charged PCPs (Figure 7B), and faster import of the shorter PCPs than the longer ones (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The effect of net charge on import rate holds true for larger native PCPs.
source: The effect of net charge seen above – faster rates for positively charged PCPs – holds true for the larger PCPs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Two major distinct events are responsible for the majority of the PCP transit time: passage of the PCP through the TOM complex and insertion of the pre-sequence through the TIM23MOTOR complex.
source: Our results suggest that two major distinct events are responsible for the majority of the PCP transit time: passage of the PCP through the TOM complex and insertion of the pre-sequence through the TIM23MOTOR complex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: The initial binding of PCP to TOM is fairly rapid.
source: By contrast, the initial binding of PCP to TOM is fairly rapid, as is passage of the mature PCP domain through TIM23.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis showing that these steps are not rate-limiting.

claim: Passage of the mature PCP domain through TIM23 is fairly rapid.
source: By contrast, the initial binding of PCP to TOM is fairly rapid, as is passage of the mature PCP domain through TIM23.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of pep86 position on import kinetics.

claim: Import appears to be largely single turnover under the experimental conditions.
source: Import appears to be largely single turnover under our experimental conditions, i.e., each import site only imports a single PCP.
evidence: This is supported by the MTX blocking experiments and comparison of imported PCP amounts to TIM23 levels.

claim: Under experimental conditions, import is limited by the amount of energy available in the form of ∆ψ.
source: We propose that, under experimental conditions, import is limited by the amount of energy available in the form of ∆ψ.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that import causes depolarisation that is not restored and that amplitude is affected by ∆ψ depletion.

claim: PCP import causes a depolarisation of the IMM that is not restored.
source: Indeed, measurements of ∆ψ using TMRM confirm that PCP import causes a depolarisation of the IMM that is not restored.
evidence: This is supported by TMRM fluorescence measurements.

claim: PCPs that require more total energy to import (such as longer ones) or that are likely to consume more ∆ψ (positively charged ones) reach a lower final concentration in the mitochondrial matrix at saturating PCP concentrations.
source: Also consistent with ∆ψ being consumed, we find that the PCPs that require more total energy to import (such as longer ones) or that are likely to consume more ∆ψ (positively charged ones) reach a lower final concentration in the mitochondrial matrix at saturating PCP concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of length and charge on amplitude.

claim: The isolated mitochondria are capable of building a PMF via respiration.
source: Importantly, we were able to show that the IMM depolarisation is an effect of import rather than an inherent problem with the mitochondria preparation. The isolated mitochondria are indeed capable of building a PMF via respiration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and furthermore, recovering PMF after dissipation caused by externally added ADP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by respirometry data.

claim: The sustained dissipation of ∆ψ is a consequence of the import process due to charge associated with the PCP itself and/or co-transporting ions.
source: Therefore, the sustained dissipation of ∆ψ must be a consequence of the import process due to charge associated with the PCP itself and/or co-transporting ions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mitochondria can build and recover PMF, but import causes sustained depolarisation.

claim: With sub-saturating levels of precursor proteins, mitochondria inside healthy cells would more easily recover their ∆ψ, enabling multiple turnovers of PCP import.
source: It is certainly conceivable that the acute addition of saturating quantities of PCP to isolated mitochondria, deployed here, overwhelms their ability to recover ∆ψ. The demand on the import apparatus in vivo would be lower. With sub-saturating levels of precursor proteins, mitochondria inside healthy cells would more easily recover their ∆ψ, enabling multiple turnovers of PCP import.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the in vivo situation based on the experimental observations.

claim: PCPs bind only to TIM23 complexes containing two Tim23 subunits and during transport this dimeric organisation becomes disrupted.
source: PCPs bind only to TIM23 complexes containing two Tim23 subunits and during transport this dimeric organisation becomes disrupted (Bauer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PCP-induced loss of ∆ψ in isolated mitochondria would prohibit the resetting of the TIM23 complex required for further turnovers.
source: Therefore, PCP-induced loss of ∆ψ in isolated mitochondria would prohibit the resetting of the TIM23 complex required for further turnovers.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the requirement for ∆ψ in TIM23 dimerisation.

claim: The transfer of PCPs from TOM to TIM23 is thought to involve cooperative interactions of subunits of the two complexes.
source: The transfer of PCPs from TOM to TIM23 is thought to involve cooperative interactions of subunits of the two complexes (Gomkale et al., 2021; Callegari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PCPs have been captured spanning both TOM and TIM23 complexes at the same time in super-complexes of ~600 kDa.
source: PCPs have been captured spanning both membrane complexes at the same time in super-complexes of ~600 kDa (Gomkale et al., 2021; Dekker et al., 1997; Gold et al., 2014; Chacinska et al., 2010), suggesting that import through TOM does not have to be complete before import through TIM23 can begin.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The in vivo existence of TOM-TIM23 super-complexes is unconfirmed.
source: Contrasting with this, however, there is also evidence to suggest that the TOM and TIM23 complexes can transport PCPs independently in steps that are not necessarily concurrent. The in vivo existence of TOM-TIM23 super-complexes is unconfirmed; they have been detected only when engineered PCPs with C-terminal domains that cannot pass through TOM are used (Chacinska et al., 2003), and only under these artificial conditions do TOM and TIM23 subunits co-immuno-precipitate or co-migrate on native polyacrylamide gels (Horst et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Direct handover from TOM to TIM23 is not absolutely required for import.
source: Our results confirm that direct handover from TOM to TIM23 is not absolutely required for import.
evidence: This is supported by the mitoplast experiments showing import can occur without the OMM.

claim: Import of proteins into mitoplasts shows that TOM and soluble factors in the IMS are dispensable for import through TIM23.
source: Import of proteins into mitoplasts, observed here and previously (Hwang et al., 1989; Ohba and Schatz, 1987; van Loon and Schatz, 1987), shows that TOM and soluble factors in the IMS are dispensable for import through TIM23.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from this study and previous studies.

claim: Transport of a PCP through TOM is reversible and therefore possible in the absence of TIM23 activity.
source: The data here also suggest that transport of a PCP through TOM is reversible and therefore possible in the absence of TIM23 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of valinomycin on k1′ and the proposed kinetic model.

claim: Retro-translocation through TOM to cytosolic proteasomes could serve as a checkpoint to ensure that the TIM23 channel does not get blocked when transport across the IMM is compromised.
source: This could serve as a checkpoint to ensure that the TIM23 channel does not get blocked when transport across the IMM is compromised.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential function of reversible transport.

claim: Proteins that are reduced or conformationally unstable in the IMS can retro-translocate to the cytosol via TOM40, and the efficiency of this process is relative to protein size.
source: For example, proteins that are reduced or conformationally unstable in the IMS can retro-translocate to the cytosol via TOM40, and the efficiency of this process is relative to protein size (both linear length and 3D complexity); smaller proteins are more efficiently retro-translocated (Bragoszewski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Under physiological conditions, PINK1 is cleaved in the IMM by PARL, releasing the C-terminal region for release back to the cytosol for proteosomal degradation.
source: Notably, under physiological conditions, PINK1 is cleaved in the IMM by PARL, releasing the C-terminal region for release back to the cytosol for proteosomal degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PINK1 processing.

claim: In bacteria, transport initiation is rapid with length-dependent passage of the mature domain rate-limiting.
source: Already the comparison of the two systems has proven to be very insightful: where, in bacteria, transport initiation is rapid with length-dependent passage of the mature domain rate-limiting (Allen et al., 2020), in mitochondria this is reversed, with slower initiation then rapid processive transport.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a previous study.

claim: In mitochondria, transport initiation is slower with rapid processive transport.
source: Already the comparison of the two systems has proven to be very insightful: where, in bacteria, transport initiation is rapid with length-dependent passage of the mature domain rate-limiting (Allen et al., 2020), in mitochondria this is reversed, with slower initiation then rapid processive transport.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the experimental data in this study.

claim: For bacteria, the rate of secretion is probably one factor limiting their ability to divide, so its optimisation will have a direct bearing on their competitiveness.
source: It is likely that these differences reflect distinct selection pressures on the two transport systems. For bacteria, the rate of secretion is probably one factor limiting their ability to divide, so its optimisation will have a direct bearing on their competitiveness.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about evolutionary pressures on bacterial secretion systems.

claim: In mitochondria, it is more critical to avoid mistargeting proteins to the matrix; hence the step where proteins are committed to matrix import is slower and more controlled.
source: Whereas in mitochondria, it is more critical to avoid mistargeting proteins to the matrix; hence the step where proteins are committed to matrix import is slower and more controlled.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about evolutionary pressures on mitochondrial import systems.
